extracted.intended_audience: researchers, research funders, policy makers, and scholars studying grant peer review and research funding processes (especially in health sciences)
extracted.subtask_description: A literature review summarizing evidence about how grant peer review works in the health sciences, including dimensions used to evaluate proposals and empirical findings about reliability, bias, process designs, and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: NIH scored review criteria (Significance, Investigators, Innovation, Approach, Environment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to NIH's 'Scored Review Criteria and Overall Impact' framework used to evaluate grant applications (commonly: Significance; Investigators; Innovation; Approach; Environment) and to derive an Overall Impact score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a scored-criteria model for evaluating proposals; referenced in the literature as an explicit multi-dimension rubric that underpins many empirical studies of peer review outcomes and reviewer language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability, fairness and validity of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation dimensions for grant peer review systems — whether review decisions are reliable (consistent across reviewers/panels), fair (free from systematic unfairness), and valid (measure what they intend to measure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple cited studies investigate these three properties in biology and medicine; they are treated as central evaluative standards when assessing peer review systems and reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threats to objectivity: bias (gender, nepotism, institutional prestige, race/ethnicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification and measurement of systematic biases that can affect review outcomes, including gender bias, nepotism, effects of university prestige, and racial/ethnic disparities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous empirical papers cited (e.g., Wenneras & Wold; Ginther et al.; Bornmann et al.; Kaatz et al.) examine these threats and their impact on funding decisions; managing or mitigating these biases is presented as a key criterion for evaluating peer review processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of panel discussion on funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which panel discussion (face-to-face or teleconference) changes initial reviewer scores and final funding decisions — e.g., panel discussion affects funding decisions for only around 10% of applications relative to original scores (as cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence comparing teleconference versus face-to-face review and analyses of discussion effects are used to judge whether panel deliberation meaningfully improves decisions or merely adds cost/time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and cost burden on applicants and reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: The time and financial costs required to prepare and review grant applications, and the broader impact on researchers' workloads and wellbeing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies cited quantify applicant time (preparation load), effects of funding deadlines on stress and family life, and costs to institutions; reducing unnecessary burden is discussed as an evaluative and policy objective (e.g., streamlined proposals, short-proposal models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of interdisciplinary research
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how peer review systems fairly and effectively assess interdisciplinary or transdisciplinary proposals, given multiple actors, settings, and criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited evidence indicates interdisciplinary research often has lower funding success and raises methodological challenges; rubric considerations include panel composition, expert matching, and criteria that capture interdisciplinary merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/risk appetite and conservatism in funding decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which review systems favor conservative, incremental work versus novel, high-risk/high-reward research, and how this affects funding of pioneering research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers on conservatism, risk-taking, and 'novelty paradox' are used to evaluate whether peer review appropriately supports innovative science or systematically disfavors it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of reviewers and inter-rater reliability (including training)
rubrics_metrics.description: How many reviewers per application are optimal and whether reviewer training improves inter-rater reliability of scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical work (e.g., on optimal reviewer number and training interventions) is cited to justify procedural design choices meant to improve consistency and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplified peer review processes and short proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of streamlined application formats (short proposals) and accelerated review procedures as alternatives intended to reduce burden and possibly speed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence from studies of short-proposal pilots and two-step reviews (e.g., NSF two-step) is discussed as a criterion for judging whether simplification maintains decision quality while lowering cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymized/blind versus open review
rubrics_metrics.description: The impact of blinding applicants' identities on reviewer judgments and funding outcomes compared to open, identified review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies of anonymized review experiments and comparisons (e.g., NSF 'Big Pitch', blind vs open review) are cited to assess whether blinding reduces bias or changes selection patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of lotteries or modified lotteries for funding allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative allocation mechanisms such as funding-by-lottery or modified lotteries as a response to low signal-to-noise in peer review rankings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical and empirical literature on lotteries is cited as a criterion to judge fairness, efficiency, and political feasibility of non-traditional allocation mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive validity of peer review scores for future productivity/impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether reviewers' scores or percentile rankings predict later citation impact, productivity, or other measures of 'return on investment'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple cohort studies comparing grant scores and later bibliometric outcomes are used to evaluate whether peer review identifies the most productive projects or investigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition and reviewer expertise influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects of reviewer expertise, selection committee membership, and panel makeup on ratings and selection success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence about reviewer expertise influencing evaluations and potential selection committee incentives ('service or self-service') is used to assess panel recruitment and composition policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest management and policy constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures and policies to manage conflicts of interest among reviewers and institutional constraints that shape decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussions of policy challenges emphasize the need to manage COI and other constraints as part of judging the integrity and fairness of peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delphi process as a review method for novel applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the Delphi consensus method as a potential solution for reviewing novel or high-uncertainty proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Delphi process is discussed as an alternative procedural rubric component when conventional peer review struggles with novelty or disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of evidence and synthesis methods (GRADE and related approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying frameworks for rating quality of evidence and strength of recommendations (e.g., GRADE) when synthesizing evidence about peer review interventions or outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referenced as an approach to appraising the evidence base about peer review practices and policy interventions; relevant when making recommendations grounded in evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consensus vs chance in peer review decision processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of consensus-building versus stochastic elements ('chance') in deciding which proposals are funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and empirical analyses probe the extent to which funding decisions reflect genuine consensus or are strongly influenced by randomness, informing acceptability of reforms (e.g., lotteries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel decision-making dynamics and team science/decision science perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: How small-team dynamics, communication, and decision science principles influence panel deliberations and outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer comments recommend considering team science and decision science literature to better understand and evaluate how panels make judgments, including personality effects and interpersonal dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative/agency-level efficiency and burden on the system
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of administrative requirements, costs, and opportunities for agencies to streamline processes to reduce overhead while preserving decision quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports and analyses (e.g., GAO) cited argue for evaluating peer review systems not just by scientific outcomes but also by administrative efficiency and cost-effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity for career stage (early career investigators) and representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of how peer review systems treat early career investigators and whether policies unintentionally disadvantage particular career stages or groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys and studies on early career funding and definitions of 'early career' are cited to inform criteria about fairness across career stages and potential policy adjustments.
